author: Jonah Chester
title: Charleston's Battery Extension project moves forward with $6.2M for design, engineering work - NewsBreak
text:
By Jonah Chester ,
1 days ago
Charleston's proposed Battery Extension would wrap around the peninsula. Areas that aren't covered by the wall would be shielded by "green" nature-based flood projects. File/Staff CHARLESTON — The Army Corps of Engineers has awarded $6.2 million for design work on two of the most visible parts of the city’s planned Battery Extension project.
The $1.3 billion Battery Extension would wrap around Charleston’s low-lying peninsula, shielding the often-flooded area from hurricane storm surge . The massive infrastructure project is a collaboration between the Army Corps (which will cover 65 percent of the project’s final cost) and the city (which will cover the remaining 35 percent).
The $6.2 million announced Sept. 29 is split between two separate contracts, both of which were awarded to the North Charleston-based Stantec-JMT Joint Venture.
The first contract ($2.91 million) will fund initial preliminary concept design for the Adger’s Wharf waterfront segment of the Battery Extension, according to a press release. That leg of the project will run from East Bay Street through Waterfront Park, and emphasize “architectural compatibility with the local historic district, using traditional materials, pedestrian-friendly gates and native plantings to preserve public harbor views and pedestrian access.”
The second contract ($3.31 million) will fund “geotechnical borings, topographical and bathymetric surveys, subsurface utility investigations and environmental analyses” along Lockwood Drive and the Ashley River. That stretch of the Battery Extension is focused on protecting the often-inundated Medical District and surrounding neighborhoods.
"Awarding these two contracts represents substantial forward momentum across both waterfronts of the peninsula," Wes Wilson, the Charleston District project manager for the Army Corps, wrote in a press release. "We are moving from high-level studies into active, on-the-ground engineering.”
There are still a few hurdles the Battery Extension needs to clear before the project breaks ground. The two contracts are part of the Preconstruction, Engineering and Design phase. City and Army Corps leaders are using this phase to come to an agreement on the precise alignment and design of the Battery Extension.
Charleston's proposed Battery Extension would wrap around the peninsula. Areas that aren't covered by the wall would be shielded by "greennature-based flood projects. File/Staff Charleston city leaders have repeatedly emphasized the need to reach an accord over aesthetics with the Corps .
“When it comes to the design, simply put, just go walk the High Battery,” Mayor William Cogswell told attendees at a July Rising Waters forum. “That is what we are modeling everything after.”
The project also needs the seal of approval from Charleston County voters. The Transportation Sales Tax referendum, on the ballot this November, would — if passed — fund about $225 million of the city’s obligation.
If the TST fails, Cogswell has said the city will need to pull the funding from elsewhere in its budget.
“The reality of it is, this can't wait,” Cogswell said in July. “We need to come up with our funding match. This piece of infrastructure — it’s too important, and time is not on our side.”
The Army Corps said residents in the Adger’s Wharf and Lockwood Drive area should expect to see “active fieldwork” in the coming weeks and months, including land surveying and water boring.
